progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m6-c05 (strong and weak; a pH meter reading; lower pH means more hydronium; one pH unit is ten times as many hydronium ions; ammonia is a weak base; NaOH a strong base; compare at the same concentration). chem-m6-c01 (H₃O⁺; acids give protons to water; bases produce OH⁻). chem-m5-p01 (validity, reliability, accuracy in plain words; risk assessment as hazard, harm, control; variables). Stage 5 (the pH scale; universal indicator). Year 11 Module 2 (concentration in mol/L).
progression.startsWith: Calibrate a pH meter and choose a range of solutions. The video opens: This pH meter has just been calibrated, and it reads distilled water as five point eight two. Shouldn't pure water be seven? So is the meter faulty?
progression.stopsAfter: choosing a range of solutions at one concentration; explaining why a pH meter needs calibrating and doing it with buffers on both sides of 7, as close to the readings as possible; carrying out the measuring routine and explaining rinsing, blotting, waiting and fresh portions; recording means; stating whether each solution has more hydronium or more hydroxide, and comparing two readings by factors of ten; explaining why open distilled water reads below 7; comparing a meter with indicator paper; naming the variables; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing the risk rows. No pH calculation (chem-m6-c07), no strength investigation (chem-m6-p04), no buffer chemistry (chem-m6-c11).
progression.nextLesson: using pH to show the difference between strong and weak acids and bases (route chem-m6-p04).

teaching.task: A freshly calibrated pH meter reads distilled water as 5.8. Is the meter wrong, the method wrong, or the water? How do you measure the pH of a range of acids and bases so the readings can be trusted, and what does each reading tell you about the ions in the sample?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a calibrated meter reads distilled water below 7: faulty, or real? (1); (2) one concentration for the acids and bases, so differences come from the substance; fresh portions in clean labelled beakers (2); (3) the glass bulb responds to hydronium ions with a small voltage; the meter turns it into pH; that link drifts with age and temperature (3); (4) so the meter is shown known values: buffers at pH 7, 4 and 10; the meter draws a straight line through those points and reads every sample from it (extended a little beyond 4 and 10); one buffer gives one point, so the slope would be guessed; buffers on both sides of 7 check the line for acids and bases; calibrate at the measuring temperature (4); (5) solution left on the probe is carried into the next sample and changes it, so rinse and blot; the glass needs time to respond, so a reading is recorded only once it stops changing; repeats use fresh portions so one contaminated portion cannot affect all three (5); (6) results as means; the acids and bases repeat closely (6); (7) below 7 more hydronium than hydroxide, above 7 more hydroxide; each step ten times, two steps a hundred; HCl about 1.4 lower than acetic acid, so in between: about 23 times the hydronium (C05 strength, recalled) (7); (8) carbon dioxide from the air dissolves and makes a little carbonic acid, which gives a few hydronium ions to the water, so open distilled water really is slightly acidic (boiling drives the CO₂ out: grey tag); with very few ions the reading drifts (8); (9) indicator paper gives about whole numbers and colour judgements vary; a meter's two decimal places mean something only if it is calibrated (9); variables (10); validity, reliability, accuracy (11); risk (12); memory aid (13); attempts and brief feedback (14 to 17); decision rule and handoff (18); key notes (19).
teaching.conversationalApproach: a freshly calibrated meter reads distilled water as 5.82, and the question of whether the meter is faulty runs through the practical. The range of solutions is matched at 0.010 mol/L so differences come from the substance; the glass bulb lens shows how hydronium makes a voltage, and calibration with pH 7, 4 and 10 buffers shows why two or more known points fix the line; the measuring routine gives a reason for each step (rinse, blot, immerse, wait for steady, three fresh readings). One class's results are read as more hydronium or more hydroxide, each pH step ten times; the water puzzle is resolved by dissolved carbon dioxide and very few ions; the meter is compared with indicator paper, then the variables, validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk assessment follow. The memory aid "Calibrate first. Rinse between. Wait for steady." closes the method. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: This pH meter has just been calibrated, and it reads distilled water as five point eight two. Shouldn't pure water be seven? So is the meter faulty? Hold that thought. In this practical you measure the pH of a range of acids and bases, and before you trust a number like this, the method has to be right.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A student measures the pH of 0.010 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution with a calibrated pH meter. Without rinsing the probe, she then measures a sample of distilled water and obtains a reading of 9.2. Other groups measured the same distilled water at about 6. Explain the difference between her reading and the other groups' readings, and describe how she should change her method." Answer: NaOH carried over on the probe added hydroxide; water has very few ions of its own, so a trace shifts its pH a lot; rinse and blot between samples, measure a fresh portion. Crossed mistake: "take three readings and average them" (without rinsing, the carried-over hydroxide still pushes the average up). (A2, Revision 2) "A student calibrates a pH meter with a pH 7.00 buffer only. She then measures the pH of 0.010 mol/L hydrochloric acid three times, using a fresh portion each time, and obtains 2.31, 2.30 and 2.32. Another group calibrated with pH 7.00 and pH 4.00 buffers and obtained 2.03 for the same solution. Evaluate the reliability and accuracy of the first student's results." Answer: reliable (range 0.02) but not accurate (about 0.3 above 2.03); with one buffer the meter assumed its slope, so every reading shares the same error; calibrate with pH 4.00 as well and repeat. Crossed mistake: "they agree, so they're accurate". Revision 1's A2 (3.4 against 5.4, "about twice") is retired: it retested C05 scene 3.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct a practical investigation to measure the pH of a range of acids and bases" this video prepares students to carry out and analyse the pH measurement practical; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: choosing a range of solutions (two acids, two bases, distilled water) at one concentration; what the meter's glass probe responds to and why calibration is needed; calibrating with buffers that cover the readings; the measuring routine (rinse, blot, immerse, wait for steady, repeat in fresh portions) and why each step matters; recording means; reading each value as hydronium against hydroxide ions, with each pH step a factor of ten; why distilled water open to air reads below 7; meter against universal indicator; variables; validity, reliability and accuracy; the risk assessment. Placement limits (playlist order 7): pH = −log[H⁺], pOH, Kw and every pH calculation are chem-m6-c07 (order 10), so no reading is calculated from a concentration and no concentration from a reading; expected values are not derived on screen. The relation to ions uses only what C05 taught (lower pH, more hydronium; one unit is ten times). Why HCl and acetic acid differ at the same concentration is C05's strength idea, recalled in one clause; testing strength with pH is chem-m6-p04 (order 8), which uses 0.100 mol/L matched solutions and a dilute-HCl challenge, so this video makes no strength conclusion and no concentration-matching argument beyond "so the difference comes from the substance". Buffers are named as "solutions that hold a known pH" only (how they work is chem-m6-c11). Water's self-ionisation is chem-m6-c06; scene 7 says only "more hydronium than hydroxide" below 7.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout (C01, C05): hydronium teal, hydroxide violet; readout amber digits; acids marked with a small teal tab on their beaker labels, bases a violet tab, water grey; controls green, hazards terracotta. Board layout (three zones, constant): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the meter and the beaker row; the right third holds the current card (routine, results table, variables, VRA, risk), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: `m6-ph-meter-probe-beaker-v1.png` (inspected 21 Oct: bench meter with a blank green screen, probe on a cable standing in a beaker of clear liquid; coded readout in the screen, as in C05), `m6-beaker-v1.png` (inspected 21 Oct: empty clear beaker; five copies with coded labels and coded colourless fills), `m6-wash-bottle-v1.png` (rinse), `m6-indicator-paper-chart-v1.png` (inspected 21 Oct: a strip and a six-colour chart, red to violet, no numbers; coded pH numbers placed under the swatches), `m5x-safety-glasses-v1.png` (risk table), `m5x-ammonia-bottle-v1.png` (risk row, the stock bottle, small, with tag "teacher only"). New plates: see Codex asset brief (three items). No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: The pH meter plate opens the hook with its readout settling at 5.82 and a ghost "7.00?" chip; the meter slides left and five labelled beakers slide into a row; the probe plate enlarges and a lens opens on the glass bulb with hydronium tokens and a millivolt needle; three buffer bottles stand in the right zone while the calibration line pins and tilts; the routine card writes one line per cue as the wash bottle stream, tissue and probe act it out; the results table fills and the chips drop onto a coded pH scale with hydronium and hydroxide bar pairs; the water beaker enlarges as carbon dioxide tokens drift in and the carbonic acid strip writes; the indicator chart and a bracket sit beside the two-decimal readout; the variables card, the three evaluation cards and the risk table write in the right zone in turn; the memory aid writes large with three icons; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the question as small plates return; the plan card and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
